en: Preface to the *Vajra-abridged Commentary*:
Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of birth and death, emerging and submerging again and again with no prospect of escape. What is the reason for this?
It is truly because the mirror of the mind is fundamentally pure and the forms reflected therein are originally void; yet sentient beings mistake them for reality. Consequently...
Giving rise to delight and aversion, producing grasping and rejecting, one creates deluded karma and willingly invites the illusory wheel of rebirth to endure suffering.
It is like seeing a tiger in a dream: both the person and the tiger are unreal. Or like flowers blooming before the eyes: both the eyes and the flowers are equally afflicted by the disease.
They cling to it and do not let go; how could there ever be an end to this? Out of compassion for them, our Buddha taught the Dharma for destroying existence, titled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
There are eight sections of the *Prajñā* in total, of which the *Vajra* is one. There are six translations of the *Vajra* in total.

Of these, the one translated by Zhi Qian is concise in expression yet rich in meaning; its phrasing is clear while its principles are profound. It truly constitutes the essential core of the eight *śāstras*.

Its ultimate aim is to shatter the false attachments to a self and to phenomena, to realize the true nature of the single mind, and to cause all sentient beings to no longer grasp at appearances, remaining as they are in unmoving suchness. When I was in my early twenties, I already knew how to read it.
I sought the meaning of this sutra in various commentaries and found my heart deeply weary of them. For while the principle is fundamentally direct, they explain it with circuitous detours;
while the phrasing is fundamentally clear, they seek it in obscure obscurity. This is largely because they are entangled in the "ivory-twigging" of the two treatises and cannot free themselves.
Yet when there are those who do not follow these two treatises, they in turn indulge in reckless sophistry.
In their hearts and minds, they have transcended the essential tenets and contravened the Buddha’s intent; thus, those who recognize this censure them.

Consequently, there are no fewer than several dozen commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā*, yet among them, one who may be called a truly excellent commentary has never been heard of. In the autumn of the year Wuxin (1201), I returned from Wuyuan to Jianyang.
While residing at Baoshan, Master Xinshi composed the *Vajra-Ṛju* (The Straightforward Vajra).
Taking Guifeng and Changshui as his primary authorities, he pruned away the redundant and extracted the essentials to facilitate the practice of beginners. He commissioned me to edit it;

although I participated in the process, I merely provided interpretations based on others and accomplished the task through their efforts. Consequently, my own mind could never find peace with it. Thus, the *Jin...* [The Golden... [is begun].

As soon as I had drafted this commentary, it inadvertently became an unfinished work. When the reforms were implemented in the spring of the Yiyou year, I grew weary of expounding on Chan and spent my days lying flat on my back.

Having no means to pass the time, I took up this sutra and commented upon it daily, completely cutting through the old-day tangles and alone revealing a brand-new sun and moon. I sought correctness in principle and clarity in expression, without any detours.
I have merely sought to rectify the flaws of obscurity and ambiguity. After three revisions of the draft, the commentary was completed. A visitor challenged me, saying:

"The ancient commentaries take the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) as their ultimate ancestor above and the Two Treatises (Madhyamaka and Yogācāra) as their foundation below; there is not a single word or character therein that does not have its source.
Now you discard them and do not follow them—is it that your wisdom can surpass that of all the Great Sages? I replied: "This is not so..."
"Nevertheless, do you say that Vasubandhu could have turned his back on Asaṅga? I say no. Do you say that Asaṅga could have turned his back on the Inner Court (the Maitreya tradition)?

I say no. Since you maintain that these three sages transmitted the teaching to one another like water being poured from one vessel to another, you ought to adhere strictly to the Master’s doctrine, just as the later disciples of Tiantai did not dare to alter even a single character. Now, observing how Vasubandhu established [his system]..."

The twenty-seven doubts already do not accord with the intention of Asaṅga; that Asaṅga divided [the stages] into eighteen abodes likewise does not accord with the words of the Inner Court (Vajrayāna). How is it that they have diverged into different paths to such an extent?
If you know that Asaṅga and Vasubandhu would certainly not have contradicted the Inner Court, then you will know that I today certainly do not contradict Asaṅga and Vasubandhu.
The guest thanked him and withdrew. I have therefore recorded this together [with his words] to serve as a preface to the beginning of the scroll.
Written by Shi-gu’s host, Shi Yuanxian, for the *Brief Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra*.
Composed by the Dharma-transmitting Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yǒngquán Chán Monastery on Gǔshān Mountain in Fúzhōu:
The Precious Names of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Its substance is most firm; no thing can destroy it. Its function is most sharp; it can...
It destroys all things; therefore, the Buddha uses it as a metaphor for the virtue of *prajñā*. *Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term, which here means "wisdom.
Its essence is the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Although it circulates through the six realms of existence, it is not diminished, being as firm as a diamond (*vajra*).
Its function is contemplative illumination; it can illuminate and shatter all things without leaving a trace, just like a diamond.
It is beneficial. Its functional capacity is designated as *pāramitā*. *Pāramitā* is also a Sanskrit term;
it is translated here as "reaching the other shore. The meaning is that saṃsāra is taken as this shore, afflictions as the middle current, and nirvāṇa as the other shore.
It is entirely through Prajñā serving as one’s boat and oar that one can leave the shore of birth and death, cross the stream of afflictions, and ascend to the shore of Nirvana.
A sūtra is a text that mirrors the mind and a vessel that carries the Way. Its meanings are:
it is taught as *dharma*, taught as *nitya*, and also taught as a path (*mārga*). *Dharma* refers to the correct track followed equally by all ten realms. *Nitya* refers to the eternal...
It is the unchanging, eternal Way. A "path" (ching) is the essential road for departing from the mundane and entering the sacred.
If this present scripture takes Prajñā as the correct track, the eternal Way, and the essential road for practitioners, it is therefore called a "sūtra."
The general purport of this sutra takes non-characteristic (*animitta*) as its fundamental principle, employing non-abiding as the skillful means.

Furthermore, it employs the six contemplations of a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, and a lightning flash as the skillful means among skillful means. First, one destroys the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*);

next, one destroys the mark of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); finally, one destroys the mark of non-phenomena (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*). Once these three are destroyed, that is itself the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), yet the true mark is without [characteristic].
Characteristics are ultimately nothing more than non-apprehension.
To realize this dharma of non-apprehension is called suchness, is called the unconditioned, is called nirvana, and is called bodhi; yet these are likewise merely names.
The full details of this matter are set forth below; let the reader examine them carefully.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

This is what the ancients called the "Preface of Certification and Faith" (samyak-pratyaya-nidāna), clarifying that the Dharma has a source from which it was received. "Thus" (evam) refers to the essence of the Dharma;

it is called "thus" (tathā) because it is neither changing nor different, and "is" (iti) because it is free from faults and transcends all that is erroneous. "I have heard" (śrutam mayā) is Ānanda’s own account of what he heard.
Although Ānanda had already realized the emptiness of the self and truly did not conceive of a self, he nevertheless followed worldly convention and provisionally [used this expression].

Because it is designated [as such], it is called "self. Since the self is ultimately without self, hearing is likewise without hearing. Because it arises from conditions, conventional designations are not destroyed;
this is precisely "hearing without hearing. As for "at one time": because the dates, months, and years differ across various regions, it is difficult to fix them definitively;
therefore, it simply says "at one time," taking the occasion when teacher and disciples were assembled and the teaching was heard to its conclusion as "one."

At that time, "Buddha" (佛)—the full term being *Buddha*—is translated here as "The Awakened One. There are three meanings to this awakening: self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening.
Śrāvastī belongs to the region of Central India. The Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Park was the vihāra where the Buddha resided;
it was located about five li to the southeast outside the city of Śrāvastī. [This was] because of Anāthapiṇḍada...
It was named because the Elder alone purchased the grove while Prince Jeta donated the trees.
"Great Bhikṣus" refers to the community that constantly follows the Buddha; "Great" is a designation for those of high seniority (*varṣāgra*) and eminent virtue. "Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term.
This is translated as "mendicant" (bhikṣu). It means that [the former] begs for the Dharma from the Buddhas above, while [the latter] begs for food from sentient beings below.
As for the one thousand two hundred and fifty people, they are Kauṇḍinya, the three Kāśyapas, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, the householder Yaśas, and their respective retinues.
All of these had previously served non-Buddhist teachers for many kalpas of hardship and toil. One...
There is nothing further to be realized. As soon as he beheld the Buddha, he immediately attained the fruit of sainthood. Moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, he constantly attended upon him.
As for the other devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, and the fourfold assembly, they are all included within the section on the dissemination of the teachings (*pravartana*).
Thus, looking from beginning to end, this is merely a concise summary.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city begging in due order, he returned to his original place. When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.

This is an account of the occasion for teaching the Dharma. The reason for teaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* by means of begging for alms is to demonstrate that the Great Dharma of *prajñā* does not transcend the midst of ordinary daily life. As for the Buddha being called the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*):

The ten titles are fully manifested, making him the Honored One among the world. As for the time of eating, it is between the hours of *chen* and *si*, because by this time the morning meal is prepared, making it convenient for both the donor and the recipient.
Regarding "putting on robes and holding the alms bowl": this has been the constant custom for begging food since the time of the Seven Buddhas.
As for "begging for food," the Buddha considers begging for food to be "right livelihood" (*samyag-ājīva*), whereas other forms of sustenance are considered "wrong livelihood" (*mithyā-ājīva*).
Therefore, it was established that bhikṣus must subsist by begging for food. That the Buddha himself now begs also has three purposes: first, to cause those who are indolent to feel shame;
second, to cause those who are arrogant to eliminate their pride; and third, to enable those who see or hear this to obtain benefit.
As for begging in sequential order, it is because the Buddha practices impartial compassion, making no distinction between the poor and the wealthy. [He] spreads...
Regarding the phrase "sitting on a seat": after the meal was finished, he was about to expound the Great Dharma.

The Qin translation simply says "sat," whereas other translations all say "entered meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). This indicates that preaching the Dharma with a distracted mind cannot accord with reality;

it must issue forth from concentration to be consistent with principle. Furthermore, a treatise states: "In other sutras, it is the attendant who spreads the seat, yet when it comes to preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha [himself does so]."
He himself spread out a seat, for he held the Prajñāpāramitā in deep reverence as the mother of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;

he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverent salutation, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all [Bodhisattvas]..."

The Bodhisattva [addressed] the Bodhisattvas: "World-Honored One, how should sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?"
The Elder is the leader among the Sangha. Subhūti is the Sanskrit name; here it is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kōngshēng).
He is also named "Well-Appeared" (Shànxiàn). Among the Buddha’s ten great disciples, he was foremost in understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The *Xiyùjì* states that Subhūti was actually the Tathāgata Śikhin of the East, who manifested his traces within the assembly of Śākyamuni to propagate the principle of emptiness. [He] bared one shoulder...
The phrase "right shoulder" and so forth represents the custom of humble respect in India. "Rare" means that it is difficult to encounter even throughout vast eons;

there is but one such being in the great trichiliocosm. Their merit and wisdom are transcendent—these three qualities are all rare. As for "Tathāgata," his essence is inherently as-it-is; he comes though there is no coming.
"Protective mindfulness" refers to the Buddha skillfully upholding the Great Dharma and mindfully protecting all bodhisattvas, causing them...
One will swiftly attain Buddhahood without the slightest hindrance. Regarding "entrustment" (*parindanā*):

it means that the Buddha skillfully entrusts the Great Dharma to the various Bodhisattvas, commanding them to continue liberating sentient beings so that the lineage shall not be severed. "Bodhisattva" is said in full to be *bodhisattva*;
this is translated as "Awakened Sentient Being. While the Buddhas are awakened and devoid of [deluded] sentiment, sentient beings possess such sentiment but have not yet awakened.
Awakening (*bodhi*). Because they possess this awakening yet still have sentient beings [to save], they are called *bodhisattvas*.
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is here translated as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Awakening," which refers to the two types of wisdom—right and universal—of all Buddhas.

Regarding the question "How should one dwell?": it asks about the state before the mind has been aroused; at that time, the mind dwells amidst sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Now that the mind has already been aroused...
Regarding the mind: upon what object should it dwell? How is it to be subdued? [The question is:
when the mind does not abide, by what means should it be subdued? This method for abiding and subduing is precisely what is meant by "skillfully protecting and skillfully entrusting."
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and subdue themselves in this manner."
"His mind was thus: 'World-Honored One, I wish most earnestly to hear.
To say 'Excellent' twice is to praise the correctness of what has been taught and to commend the essential nature of the question asked;
it is able to bring broad benefit to the great assembly and to those of the future. 'Listen attentively' is an admonition that one must not employ a mind subject to arising and ceasing."
This refers to listening to the Dharma of true reality (*dharmatā*).
Such a person points directly to *prajñā* (wisdom), meaning they should abide solely in this Dharma and subdue their mind through this Dharma.

If it were otherwise, that which one abides in would be a delusory realm, and the act of subduing the mind would itself become a delusory mind; furthermore, how could one ever attain unsurpassed *bodhi*?
"Truly so. These words are expressions of compliance. Although [Subhūti] has already grasped the general meaning, he has not yet heard the details;
therefore, he requests them again.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. Whatever..."
Of all classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;

whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation.
This is a detailed response to the questions posed. Although there were two questions, the Buddha answered them collectively.
His intention was that one must solely subdue the mind and not allow it to become attached to signs (*nimitta*); furthermore, one must not seek elsewhere for a separate dharma in which to abide.
Therefore, he first sets forth "subduing the mind" and later concludes with "one should abide as instructed. The passage beginning with "All... speaks of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Vast and profound—this is precisely what is called the bodhicitta. "Womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born" refers to the distinctions among births within the three realms.
Heaven and hell belong exclusively to the transformation-born; the hungry ghosts include both womb-born and transformation-born; humans and animals possess all four modes of birth.

"Those with form" refers to the devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); "those without form" refers to the devas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Those with perception" [refers to those possessing mental cognition].
"Those" refers to the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). "Non-perception" refers to the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

"Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). *Nirvāṇa*—here translated as "extinction and deliverance" (*mièdù*)—means the extinction of the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling and the crossing over of the two kinds of birth-and-death.
It is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) because it constitutes the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood, beyond which there is nothing further.

It refers to the "remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa). Since it is said that all shall be made to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and yet also said that they are "extinguished and delivered" (*parinirvṛta*), this is a case where both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together. Now, the faculties and natures of all sentient beings are not the same;
how could they all enter nirvana? It is because all who possess a mind will certainly become Buddhas. For one who has resolved upon the vast mind—how could it be otherwise?
There are some who are left behind; however, those whose roots of goodness are matured are immediately delivered and liberated. Those who are not yet matured are first caused to reach maturity.
Even for those in the eight difficult circumstances, he skillfully plants the seeds for them so that they may be delivered at a later time.
In this way, he brings to parinirvāṇa immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; yet, in reality, there is no sentient being who has been brought to parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span...
Then they are not Bodhisattvas.
This says that although the Bodhisattva’s resolve to deliver sentient beings is exceedingly vast and profound, in reality, not a single sentient being attains extinction.
This is because the Bodhisattva does not linger in signs. If one possesses the four signs, [one is not a Bodhisattva].

This means there would be a savior and those to be saved; these are merely ordinary worldlings within the cycle of birth and death. How could they be called Bodhisattvas? This section represents the Buddha’s response to the question:
one should take the signless (*animitta*) as that in which one should abide, and take that which possesses signs (*sanimitta*) as that which should be subdued.

Regarding the four marks (*catur-nimitta*): according to the treatise, identifying the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as "self" and "what belongs to the self" is called the mark of self (*ātma-nimitta*). To calculate that the self is born...

The distinction of a person from other realms of existence is called the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). To conceive that the self arises from the gathering together of the five aggregates and other phenomena is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
To conceive that the self undergoes a single lifetime of retribution with its life-force remaining uninterrupted is called the mark of a life-span (*jīva-nimitta*).
These constitute one general mark of a self, which is divided into four. However, the foolish claim that this sutra teaches the absence of these four marks; this is not the case.

This explains the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*). As it is said, "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa," it follows that there are not only no sentient beings, but also no nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, as stated in the passage below: "If one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one is attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span;
if one grasps at the marks of non-dharmas, one is likewise attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. From this we know:
The wondrous light of Prajñā penetrates directly through the three emptinesses; how could it be limited merely to the emptiness of persons?
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without abiding in anything regarding dharmas.

That is to say, one should not abide in form when practicing giving, nor should one abide in sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should act thus...
This is giving. It does not abide in signs (*nimitta*).
What was stated above—that there should be no signs—does not mean that signs are extinguished or made non-existent; it simply means not abiding in them.
This non-abiding precisely demonstrates the method of subduing. Now, this will be clarified by way of practice. Regarding "in the dharmas," this is a general heading for the six [perfections].
Dust. There are three kinds of giving: the gift of material goods (*āmiṣadāna*), the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), and the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

These three gifts can encompass the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), and the six perfections extensively encompass all practices. Therefore, we now cite the single perfection of giving to include them all.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) up to awakening (*bodhi*), one should abide in nothing at all. Now, we shall simply speak of...
The six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are also mentioned here by citing one to include all;
why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit cannot be measured or conceived.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the empty space in the eastern direction be measured or conceived? "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, [it is likewise with the merit of such giving].
"Can the emptiness of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling on signs is likewise immeasurable.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed."

The interlocutor asks: "For what reason must one practice giving without dwelling on signs? [The response is: Because when one practices giving without dwelling on signs, the giving accords with the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
Since this emptiness of intrinsic nature is boundless, the merit is likewise boundless. Below, the text cites the empty space of the ten directions as an analogy.
This correctly illustrates the boundlessness of merit. There are two meanings: first, it illustrates vastness and inexhaustibility; second, it illustrates ultimate and endlessness.
"One should simply abide as instructed" does not mean abiding alone; it truly means that by abiding, one simultaneously subdues the mind.
The Buddha’s intention is that the mark of abiding is itself the deluded mind, whereas non-abiding is [the true state].
Subdue. Once the deluded mind is subdued, one transcends and abides nowhere; this is precisely that which should be dwelt upon.
Having finished answering the two questions, the Buddha further provides a detailed resolution below, fearing that people might give rise to doubts based on the literal words.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Whatever marks exist are all empty and false. If one perceives that all marks are non-marks...”
He then beheld the Tathāgata.
Previously, it was stated that one should not dwell upon signs. Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might doubt this, wondering:

"If one does not dwell upon signs, how can one become a Buddha and yet possess physical marks? Therefore, he raised this point to question Subhūti. Subhūti replied: "One cannot perceive [the Buddha] by means of his physical marks."

He beheld the Tathāgata. Since the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are accomplished based on the purified aspect of the *paratantra* (dependent nature), and because the *paratantra* is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the body is itself no-body.
When Kṣemadatta had thus realized that the Buddha’s body is without marks, the Buddha further instructed him, saying:
"Whatever has marks is entirely illusory. Therefore, although it is the Buddha’s body, it is likewise illusory; yet, it is not...
One may grasp that marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are false and illusory, and seek separately for a Buddha who is markless.

However, by realizing the non-markedness within the very midst of marks, one immediately perceives the Tathāgata. Since all marks have thus vanished, there remains only the essence of awakening (*bodhi*). It is like a reflection appearing in a mirror:
when one realizes the reflection is entirely empty, one sees only the mirror itself. This is precisely the esoteric intent of the present sutra; students should understand it well.
[The Buddha] contemplates this.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti, “Do not speak thus. After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, during the final five hundred years...”
"Furthermore, Ānanda, there may be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit who are able to give rise to faith in these words and take them as true.
You should know that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
they have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas."
The preceding statement that it is not by seeing marks that one sees the Tathāgata is a meaning of profound depth; therefore, Subhūti gave rise to doubt. Those with true faith are truly rare.
"True faith" means to directly penetrate and shatter all phenomena—whether defiled or pure, existent or non-existent—and to enter into silent resonance with the true mark (*dharmatā*).
The Buddha said: "Do not say that there are no people of true faith today; they exist even within the final five hundred years."
In every age, there will also be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit who are able to give rise to true faith within this Dharma. Why is this?
It is because such persons possess deep and profound roots of goodness, having planted various roots of virtue under immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas.
As for the "five hundred years," during the first five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, liberation shall be firm; during the second...

During the first five hundred years, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) will be firm; during the second five hundred years, ethical discipline (*śīla*) will be firm; during the third five hundred years, extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) will be firm;
during the fourth five hundred years, stūpas and monasteries (*vihāra*) will be firm; and during the fifth five hundred years, strife and contention will be firm.
When the Sūtra speaks of "the latter five hundred years," it refers to this fifth period.
"Subhūti, those who hear these phrases and give rise to even a single thought of pure faith—such beings, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees;
they shall obtain such immeasurable merit."

"Pure faith" (śraddhā) is faith free from all defilement and attachment; it is also true faith. If there is a person whose past merit is profound and thick, they may give rise to even a single thought of pure faith.
Although that faith is extremely subtle, the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom and Buddha-eye, can fully know and see it.
Its merit is immeasurable—how much more so for one who possesses perpetual faith! It must be said thus.
As for those who come to know and see: because they are not like the Tathāgata, none are able to know or see the greatness of his merit.
Why is this? It is because these sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span;
they have no mark of dharmas, nor do they have any mark of non-dharmas. Why is this? Because if these sentient beings were to grasp at marks with their minds, they would immediately become attached.
If one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one is attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this?
If one grasps at the marks of non-dharmas, one is likewise attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
The interlocutor asks: For what reason does a single moment of pure faith immediately yield such immeasurable merit?

It is because the mind accords with *prajñā*; all false attachments are completely eliminated. Consequently, there is no longer any grasping at a self, a person, or other such identities within the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Nor is there any appearance of the phenomena of the five aggregates themselves. Furthermore, there is no appearance of non-phenomena, such as the negation of the five aggregates. This is the nature of dharmas.

"Characteristics" refers to everything from the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) up to enlightenment (*bodhi*) and nirvana—all that possesses names and characteristics.
"The characteristic of non-dharmas" refers to the teaching that from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases up to enlightenment and nirvana, none of these can be apprehended.
Again, it is asked: "If the four marks are certainly non-existent, why are the characteristics of dharmas and non-dharmas also [non-existent]?"
It must be non-existent. For if the mind grasps at signs, it is precisely to become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
The two phrases "if the mind grasps at signs" state in general that the marks of dharmas and non-dharmas are not to be grasped; the following then explains this specifically.

That is to say, although one does not identify the five aggregates and other such dharmas as a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, one merely grasps at the existence of the five aggregates.

"Equal dharmas" refers precisely to attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Since all dharmas possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they can certainly be objects of attachment.
As for what is "non-dharma," it has no characteristics to which one could be attached; why, then, must even this be negated?

Because if one establishes a characteristic based on the characteristic of "non-cause," or maintains a state of "removing the non-existent," this is still attachment to characteristics. Therefore, even this must be negated. This section was traditionally interpreted by many as the "Three Emptinesses."

I shall explain this. My humble opinion is that it is not so. Since the four marks have already been elucidated in depth previously, this passage merely clarifies that neither *dharma* nor *adharma* should be grasped.
Therefore, the subsequent text immediately follows by stating: "For this reason, one should not grasp at *dharma*, nor should one grasp at *adharma*.
Thus, the purport becomes even more clear.
Therefore, you should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should you grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata has always said:
"O bhikṣus, understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like a raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
Continuing from the preceding text, it is said that both the Dharma and non-Dharma should not be grasped. For this reason, the Tathāgata has often said:
"The Dharma I have taught is exactly like a raft. A raft is used for crossing a river, but once the shore is reached, it is abandoned;
one must not constantly cling to it. All the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are established as skillful means (*upāya*) to deliver all beings.
Sentient beings do not truly exist; how could one cling to them without relinquishing them? "Even phenomena (*dharma*) should be relinquished, how much more so what is non-phenomena (*adharma*).
This means that the teaching of emptiness is solely for the purpose of crossing over existence. Once the river of existence has been crossed, emptiness itself must also be emptied.
If even existence must be emptied, how much more so can emptiness not be emptied?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught..."
There is no fixed dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak of.
Why is this? All dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this so? Because all noble sages attain their distinctions through the dharma of non-activity (*asaṃskṛta*).
The preceding statement says there is no dharma and no non-dharma. Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might doubt whether he had ever attained bodhi or ever preached the Dharma, wondering:
"Is it not the case that there exists a dharma that can be grasped and can be spoken? Therefore, he raised this as a question for Subhūti.
Subhūti deeply comprehended the Buddha’s intention and thus replied: "There is no fixed dharma named Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
In the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*), there is likewise no fixed dharma that can be taught. That which is "without a fixed dharma" means there is no single, real, fixed dharma.
Why is there no single, real, fixed dharma? Because all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata cannot be grasped through names or characteristics;
at the very moment they are heard, they are not heard. They cannot be expressed through speech; at the very moment they are spoken...
There is nothing to be said. Since it cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken, how could there be any talk of "Dharma" or "non-Dharma"?
Furthermore, it is asked: why can this Dharma not be grasped or spoken? It is because it is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma.
As for the unconditioned Dharma, its wondrous essence is profound and tranquil; it fundamentally lacks names and characteristics and does not involve language, transcending even the concept of "one."
All conceptual discriminations regarding conditioned phenomena are what all sages and worthies have equally realized; there is merely a distinction therein of shallow and deep, or great and small.
This sutra first destroys appearances (lakṣaṇa) for fear that people might cling to appearances; subsequently, it destroys emptiness (śūnyatā) for fear that people might cling to emptiness.
When both emptiness and appearance are empty, one finally accords with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). This is called the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Thus, the meaning of *prajñā* is fully exhausted. Subhūti, what do you think?

If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied: "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because this merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
As stated above, when the wondrous wisdom of prajñā penetrates directly to the three emptinesses and suddenly realizes the unconditioned, how could its merit ever be exhausted?
Thus, the World-Honored One cites the merit of giving precious jewels to manifest its superiority over the merit of the trichiliocosm.
A thousand worlds constitute a small chiliocosm; a thousand small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm; and a thousand medium chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm.

They all arise and perish simultaneously. As for the statement that "this merit is not the nature of merit," it means that this merit lacks inherent nature and is thus the emptiness of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Therefore, when the Tathāgata speaks of "much merit," he refers to that which is not [inherently existent] merit.
To say that the merit is great refers to what exists conventionally (*saṃvṛti*). If one were to grasp it as being substantially real (*dravyasat*), how could that be the intention of the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, if there should be someone who receives, upholds, and even teaches as few as four lines of verse from this sutra to others, [the merit would be immeasurable].
The merit of this [person] surpasses that [of the former]. Why is this?
Subhūti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas issue forth from this sūtra. Subhūti, what is called "Buddha-dharma" is as follows:
This is not the Buddha’s Dharma.
Although the merit from giving away the treasures of a great trichiliocosm is vast, in reality it is insufficient to be called much.
If, however, there should be someone who receives and upholds even as little as a four-line stanza from this sutra and explains it to others, their merit would be superior.

He asked: "For what reason can the recitation and upholding of a single verse surpass that? Although the merit from giving jewels may be vast, it ultimately remains within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*).
Yet the power of upholding this sutra is able to purify and eliminate all attachments and bring the ultimate fruit to perfection.
It is because all Buddhas and all the dharmas taught by all Buddhas emerge from this sutra."

Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might become attached to the Buddha-dharma; therefore, he followed by sweeping away its traces, saying: "That which is called the Buddha-dharma is not, in fact, the Buddha-dharma.

According to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there exist delusion and enlightenment, defilement and purity, and the ordinary person and the sage; thus it is said that the Buddha-dharma emerges from the scriptures.
However, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one is free from delusion and enlightenment, defilement and purity, and the ordinary person and the sage. How could it abide?
It is possible for the Buddha-dharma to emerge from the sūtras. The power of faith is called "receiving" (śraddhā), and the power of mindfulness is called "retaining" (dhāraṇī).
Regarding the "four-line verse," discussions have long been confused and varied, with each person selecting four lines from within the sūtras to serve as the standard.

They fail to realize that there are the words "even as few as" (yāvad eva) at the beginning; this signifies the intention of going from many to few. It means that one should receive [the teaching] from this sūtra...
"Uphold and expound"—this refers generally to those who receive and uphold [the text], whether it be a complete fascicle, half a fascicle, a single section, or even as little as a four-line verse.
Furthermore, it is incorrect to interpret the word "etc. (*ādi*) as encompassing the subsequent hundreds of thousands of verses;
for the intent of the sutra is fundamentally to proceed from the many to the few, not from the few to the many.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna (stream-enterer) have the thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of stream-entry’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A srotāpanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore he is called a srotāpanna.”

The preceding statement declared that the Dharma cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken. The Buddha feared that people might suspect that the Śrāvakas each grasp their own respective fruits and speak according to their realization;
would this not then imply there is grasping and speaking? He therefore raised this as a question for Subhūti, and Subhūti replied to all of them with "No.
Furthermore, he explained for each case that what appears to be grasping is fundamentally without grasping, and what appears to be speaking is fundamentally without speaking.
This is the intended meaning. Regarding the first fruit of the Śrāvaka: having severed eighty-one *kleśas* (proclivities) of coarse, discriminative delusion, one is named *Srotāpanna*.

In Chinese, this is translated as "Entering the Stream," meaning that one has for the first time entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*). It does not mean that there is some separate, real entity into which one enters;
rather, it is simply called "entering the stream" because one no longer enters the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and is thus no longer led astray by them.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have this thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A sakṛdāgāmin is so called because he returns once more;
yet in reality there is no coming or going. It is for this reason that he is called a sakṛdāgāmin.”
Regarding the two fruits of the Śrāvaka: one who has severed the six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm is called a *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Flower: "One Who Returns Once").
This means that after passing away from this life, they go once to the heavens and return once to the human world before attaining the state of an *Anāgāmin*;

thus, they are named "One Who Returns Once. In reality, there is no such coming or going; having already realized the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*), who is there to come or go? Although [the conventional designation] is not discarded...
They come and go, yet they do not conceive of coming and going.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought: "I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin"?
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? An Anāgāmin is called 'one who does not come,' and yet—"
In reality, there is no one who does not come; for this reason, he is called an Anāgāmin.
Among the three fruits of the Śrāvaka, one who has severed the nine grades of afflictions of desire is named an Anāgāmin; in Chinese, this is translated as "One Who Does Not Come."
This means that having passed away from this life, one is reborn in the heavens and does not return to take birth in the lower realms; therefore, they are called "Non-returners" (Anāgāmin).
Yet, in reality, there is no such thing as a "non-returner. Since there is already no self, who is it that does not return?
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does an arhat have this thought: ‘I have attained the path of an arhat’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? Because, in reality, there is no dharma called ‘arhat.’”
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," he would immediately be attached to a self,
a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
As for the four fruits of the Śrāvaka, one is called an Arhat when they have exhausted all seventy-two grades of afflictions of the upper two realms.
An Arhat possesses three meanings: first, "one who has no enemies," because the afflictions of views and thoughts have been exhausted;

second, "one who is not born," because having severed birth-and-death within the realm of limited segments, they do not undergo further existence; third, "one worthy of offerings," because they are capable of receiving the great offerings of devas and humans.
"In reality there is no dharma" means that in reality there is nothing to be attained. If there were even a single thought of attainment—
If one harbors a mind toward the fruits [of the path], one is immediately attached to the marks of a self, persons, and so forth; how then could one possibly attain realization?
Among these four fruits, only the Arhat alone is named "one who has attained the Way," because the other three fruits have not yet fully attained that Way.
“World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention and am foremost among men;
that I am an arhat free from desire. World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as, ‘I am an arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as, ‘I have attained the path of arhatship,’ then the World-Honored One would not say of me, Subhūti, that I delight in emptiness.”
Regarding the practice of *araṇā* (non-contention): because Subhūti truly has no practice, he is called "Subhūti who delights in the practice of *araṇā*.

When the previous Buddha questioned him regarding the four fruits of the spiritual life, Subhūti replied on both occasions that he had not attained them; here, he again cites himself as proof. Thus said the Buddha.
Regarding the statement that he has attained the *araṇā-samādhi*: because he understands emptiness (*śūnyatā*), both self and other are forgotten;
thus, he is able not to afflict sentient beings, and can also cause sentient beings not to give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it says he is "the foremost among men":
because within the human realm the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) have not yet been eliminated, all possess contention (*raṇa*); now, since he is without contention, he is...
He is the foremost among men. Regarding "one who has abandoned desire": the craving within the three realms is collectively termed "desire";
now that this has been completely extinguished, he has truly become an Arhat. From the words "I do not have such thoughts" below, the meaning of the Buddha’s praise is explained:
because he is without self (*anātman*). *Araṇa* means "tranquility. He says, "I have attained Arhatship."
If one has not yet forgotten the four marks [of conditioned existence], afflictions will arise in confusion; how then could this constitute the practice of tranquility?

One who truly practices nothing is one for whom the mark of self is already empty; thus, although there is something practiced, in reality there is nothing practiced—this is the practice of tranquility.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, was there any dharma that he obtained?
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, in reality there was no dharma that he obtained."

Previously, it was clarified that there is nothing to be attained in any of the four fruits of the path. Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might doubt whether he had received the Dharma from Dīpaṃkara, thinking, "Is this not an instance of grasping and teaching?
Therefore, he raised this as a question for Subhūti. Subhūti replied that, in reality, there is nothing to be attained;
for what was taught by Dīpaṃkara is what Śākyamuni heard, and thus they were in accord through non-conceptual wisdom.
When one discerns the principle, wisdom merges with the principle and the object unites with the spirit; how could there be any trace of verbal expression?
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called adorning a buddha-field is not truly adorning; it is merely named 'adorning.'
Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might suspect that a bodhisattva’s adornment of a buddha-field implies a grasping nature;
therefore, he raised this as a question for Subhūti. A "buddha-field" refers to the land of recompense obtained at the time of attaining Buddhahood.
"Adornment" refers to the various kinds of embellishments within that field, all of which result from the myriad practices of the bodhisattva. This is the intended meaning of Subhūti’s reply.
This means that when a bodhisattva is endowed with the myriad practices of the six perfections, they adorn the Buddha-lands while their mind remains free from attachment.
They practice without practicing; both the adornment and that which is adorned are ungraspable. Thus, it is an adornment that is not an adornment—this is what is called "adorned Buddha-lands."
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms;
they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. They should give rise to their minds by dwelling nowhere at all.
Continuing from the preceding text, that which is "not solemn yet solemn" refers to the generation of a pure mind. As for what is called generating a pure mind:
one should not allow the mind to arise by dwelling upon the objects of the six sense-fields; rather, one should generate a mind that dwells nowhere.
When one generates a mind that dwells nowhere, then one acts without acting. This is what is meant by being "solemn yet not solemn."
Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be considered great?

Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One. "Why is this? [the Buddha asked]. "Because the Buddha has said that what is called 'body' is not a body; it is merely designated as 'great.'"

[Regarding] the body: Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might doubt that the Tathāgata has received a retributive body (*vipākakāya*), and wonder, "Is this not an act of grasping? Therefore, he raised this as a question for Subhūti.
Subhūti also replied, "It is exceedingly great," and further explained himself, saying: "If one relies upon ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), then the retributive..."
The body is empty; fundamentally, it is not a body. Furthermore, that which is called a "great body" is spoken of only in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges—what do you think? [Would those be many?]
"What do you think? Are all those Ganges rivers many? Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Those Ganges rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands. "Subhūti, I now tell you the truth:
if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges rivers..."
"If one were to give as a gift a thousand worlds, would the merit obtained be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even recite as little as a four-line verse for the sake of others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."
This is a comparison intended to manifest superiority. As for the Ganges River: it is forty *li* in circumference, with golden sand flowing within its waters, as fine as flour.

Because the Buddha’s vihāra is near this river, it is used as a metaphor. First, consider the sands of a single Ganges River—counting one Ganges River for each grain of sand—and they are already immeasurably many;
how much more so, then, the sands of all such Ganges Rivers? How could [the number of Buddhas] possibly be compared?

There is a measure: suppose one were to take the sands of all the Ganges Rivers, and for every single grain of sand, calculate one great trichiliocosm, and fill them all with the seven treasures to give as alms; in this way, the worlds would be inexhaustible and the seven treasures would be inexhaustible.
Yet, how vast would that merit be? Nevertheless, the merit of upholding this sutra truly surpasses that. Why is this? Because...

Although the giving of jewels may be vast, if the four marks [of self, person, sentient being, and life] have not been forgotten, one will merely obtain the blessings and retributions of humans and devas.
However, through the merit of upholding this sutra, one can realize the dual emptiness of persons and phenomena and directly achieve unsurpassed bodhi;

this cannot be compared in the same breath with the giving of jewels. The calculation and comparison herein are even more superior than the previous one, for the former spoke only of a single trichiliocosm.
"Jeweled Giving. This refers to the giving of jewels throughout immeasurable trichiliocosms. By means of this passage, it is taught that the four fruits [of the path] are mindless;

Śākyamuni has no attainment; the adornment and purification of the buddha-field is adorned without being adorned; and the cultivation and realization of the Buddha-body is realized without being realized.
These matters are beyond the scope of the preceding text; therefore, this comparison is even more superior than what came before.

Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by the entire world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it? Subhūti, you should know that such persons have accomplished the most supreme, foremost, and rare [attainment].
Regarding the existence of this Dharma: wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha and there are honored disciples.
This clarifies the supreme merit of the sutra. *Stūpa* is a Sanskrit term; in this [Chinese] language, it means "lofty and manifest.

It refers to something that reaches the clouds and towers above the Han lands, so that those who see it from afar or nearby may generate merit. *Miao* (temple) refers to appearance; it refers to the hall within.

This refers to the physical form of the Buddha. The underlying meaning is that even a place where one merely recites a four-line verse is worthy of worship by all devas and humans alike, just like a stupa or temple of the Buddha;
how much more so for a person who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite the entire sutra?
Such a person is not limited to being at such a place alone; the act of receiving and upholding the entire sutra is likewise not limited to that location.
This is a single verse. One should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma.
"Most supreme" means proceeding directly toward unsurpassed Bodhi. "Foremost" means far transcending all other vehicles. "Rare" means...
It is peerless in the world. Such is the merit obtained by those who receive and uphold this sutra.
Even if there were no one to receive and uphold it, wherever this scripture exists, there is also a Buddha and his disciples.

Since the sutra explains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and based on the Dharma there are the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), where there are Buddhas of these three bodies, there must necessarily be worthy and holy disciples.
"Son, wherever this sutra exists, the Three Jewels will always remain. It shall be venerated by humans, devas, and others;
how then can there be any doubt?
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should we uphold it?'"
"Uphold it. The Buddha told Subhūti, "This sūtra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is that? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls *prajñāpāramitā* is not actually *prajñāpāramitā*; it is merely designated as *prajñāpāramitā*."
Having heard that the merit of receiving and upholding this sutra is so great, Subhūti requested to receive and uphold it by its name.
"Vajra" carries the meaning of being both firm and sharp; the essence and function of Prajñā are like this.
As for "Pāramitā," it refers to crossing over all suffering and distress through the power of Prajñā. Why was this name established? It was necessary.
Know this: names are established to represent reality; one must not cling to the name and thereby lose the reality.
This very name is not that name, for the nature of names is empty and nothing can be apprehended therein—this is the meaning of "reality.
Furthermore, when it is said, "This is that name," it is merely borrowing a name to manifest it. One should uphold it in this manner. Thus it is.
This refers to those who uphold it well.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has nothing to preach.

Since the Buddha had established this title for the sutra, he feared that people might suspect the Buddha actually possessed some dharma to preach; therefore, he raised this point to question Subhūti.
Subhūti replied: "The Tathāgata has nothing to preach" because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is beyond all dependence, and it is the ultimate reality.
There are no words. Whatever is spoken is, by its very nature, fundamentally empty and quiescent; thus, although there is speaking, in reality there is nothing spoken.
The subsequent text enumerates in detail the speaking of atoms, the speaking of worlds, and the speaking of the thirty-two marks, all of which clarify the principle that there is nothing spoken.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has spoken of are not atoms;
they are called 'atoms. The world-systems which the Tathāgata has spoken of are not world-systems; they are called 'world-systems.'"
Among all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is nothing more minute than the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*), and nothing more vast than the world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Yet, the subtle atom lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the world-system likewise lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said that the subtle atom is not a subtle atom, and the world-system is not a world-system;
they are merely called "subtle atoms" and "world-systems" because they are produced through false conditions (*mithyā-pratyaya*). Now, as for the subtle atom...
If even dust and worlds do not exist at all, how could that which the Buddha has taught possess any reality?
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? Because that which the Tathāgata calls the thirty-two...
The two marks are themselves non-marks; this is called the thirty-two marks.
The Buddha feared that people might doubt his previous statement that the worlds of motes are insentient and thus lack real nature.
He thought, "If the Buddha's body were sentient, how could one say it lacks [real nature]? Therefore, he raised this question to Subhūti. Subhūti replied:
He said: "One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. For these thirty-two marks are accomplished through dependence and lack intrinsic nature;
therefore, they are called 'non-marks. It is only by means of the mark of non-mark that [the Tathāgata is perceived]."
It is merely designated as the "thirty-two marks. Now, if even the Buddha’s body is not existent, how could that which the Buddha has taught possess any reality?
