The Buddha said, "It is the same for a bodhisattva. If one says, "I shall deliver sentient beings," there is a bodhisattva;
yet, such a one is not a bodhisattva, because in reality there is no dharma that can be named a bodhisattva. Therefore, the following cites previous words to prove this: "All dharmas are..."
There are no four marks, because all dharmas are suchness.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva should form this thought, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he is not called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said: "That which is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is itself not an adornment; it is merely named 'adornment.
If one says, 'I shall practice the ten thousand practices to adorn the Buddha-lands,' then there is a bodhisattva, yet he is not a true bodhisattva.
It is by means of non-adornment that one adorns; only then is it truly adornment."
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata declares him to be a true bodhisattva.

While the previous two statements indicated that there are bodhisattvas who are not bodhisattvas, this passage correctly clarifies that those who are not bodhisattvas are designated as "bodhisattvas."
This is because they have attained penetration into the dharma of selflessness (*anātman*). There are two kinds of selflessness: first, the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*);
second, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Both the self and phenomena are fundamentally non-existent; it is simply necessary to penetrate this.

If one does not penetrate it, then emotional attachments will arise within the midst of quiescent equality, whereby there is a "self" that seeks to save itself and adorn itself. If, however, one does penetrate it, then one accords with the nature within the realm of pure and sublime merit.
The Manifestation: It is clearly evident that it is neither austere nor transcendent; thus, while the myriad practices boil forth, not even a speck of dust is established.
While the single truth is concentrated and still, all virtues shine resplendently. This is what is called a true Bodhisattva.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? "Yes, [World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye]."
“Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
The previous statement that there are no bodhisattvas was made because they have realized the non-self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*).
The Buddha feared that people might doubt how it could be said that there are no sentient beings when sentient beings cannot realize the non-self of persons and phenomena;

therefore, he extensively explains this by means of what is seen by the five eyes, clarifying that sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings. As for the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), it is the fleshly eye of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Buddha’s flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) sees countless worlds within obstructed spaces. As for the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), it is drawn forth from the locus of the flesh eye.
The divine eye of ordinary beings sees only what is beyond obstructions; the divine eye of those of the Two Vehicles sees only the trichiliocosm;
the Buddha’s divine eye can see the subtle forms of all the devas as well as worlds as numerous as the sands of countless rivers.

Regarding the realms: those with the wisdom-eye use fundamental gnosis to illumine the principle of true emptiness. Those of the two vehicles illumine only the emptiness of persons, whereas Bodhisattvas can illumine the emptiness of phenomena;
however, this is but a partial realization. Only the Buddha perfectly illumines the three types of emptiness, leaving nothing unexhausted.

The Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) refers to the teaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). The followers of the Two Vehicles do not possess the Dharma-eye;
for while Bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted all that is to be known, their realization differs at each stage (*bhūmi*). Only a Buddha has exhausted the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);

there is nothing he does not know and no being he does not deliver. The Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) is simply the aforementioned four eyes as they exist in a Buddha, so named because they are all supreme therein.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River truly sands, as the Buddha has described them?
"Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has described them as sands. "Subhūti, what do you think?

If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and if one were to take the number of grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that constitute a great number of Buddha-worlds?"
"So it is. Would that not be much? "It would be very much, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that all minds are 'no-minds';
they are called 'minds' [only] by name."
This clarifies the successive range of what is seen by the five eyes, which consists of five stages.
First, the sands of a single Gaṅgā River are counted. Second, the rivers are counted by means of their sands. Third, the world-systems are counted by means of the sands of immeasurable rivers.
Fourth, all sentient beings within those world-systems are counted. Fifth, the various minds within all those sentient beings are counted. All of these [are known] by the Buddha.
That which is clearly seen by the five eyes knows that all minds are in fact no-mind; this is what is called "mind.
Since mind is already no-mind, sentient beings are fundamentally quiescent; how, then, could there be any sentient beings?
Why is that? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended;
and the future mind cannot be apprehended.
This interrogates and explains the meaning of "non-mind. That which is called "non-mind" means that it cannot be apprehended across all three periods of past, present, and future.
For the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arisen, and the present does not abide.
Furthermore, it is merely a false discrimination; what, then, could be pointed to as "mind"?

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this cause, acquire much merit? "So it is, World-Honored One.
That person, by reason of this cause, would acquire very much merit. "Subhūti, if merit had any substantial reality, the Tathāgata would not say that one acquires merit."
The merit is great. Because there is no [intrinsic] merit, the Tathāgata says that one obtains great merit.

Previously, it was stated that the three minds are ungraspable; the Buddha feared that people might doubt this, thinking that if the mind is ungraspable, then the basis for performing merit—which arises from the mind—is likewise non-existent, and thus they would abandon the cultivation of merit. Therefore, he raised the example of the gift of jewels to question Subhūti.
Śāriputra already understood the Buddha’s intention; therefore, he answered that his merit was great.

The World-Honored One further clarified this meaning, stating that if one does not penetrate the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and clings to things as real, then the mind has a point of attachment. Consequently, the merit becomes contaminated (*sāsrava*) and cannot be called "great.
However, if one penetrates the emptiness of intrinsic nature and does not cling to things as real, then the mind has no point of attachment. Thus, the merit becomes [uncontaminated].
The untainted [dharmas] may indeed be said to be many. Thus we know that one must not neglect merit and fail to cultivate it; rather, what is valued is cultivation without dwelling upon signs.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Buddha be seen by means of a body endowed with physical form? "No, World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection of the physical body (*rūpakāya*). Why is this?

The Tathāgata has said that the perfection of the physical body is itself not the perfection of the physical body; it is merely designated as the "perfection of the physical body. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*)? "No, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the possession [of the marks]."

[One] perceives various marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said: "That which is called being endowed with all marks is, in fact, not being endowed [with them]; it is merely designated as 'being endowed with all marks.

Previously, it was stated that there is no measure to the merit, for its merit is vast. This was said because one might otherwise suspect that the Buddha’s physical marks and signs of excellence were produced solely by his own merit.
That which the Buddha has accomplished consists of the marks and signs by which one may perceive the Tathāgata; therefore, the Buddha raised these as questions for Subhūti:
the physical body endowed with the eighty minor marks, and the various marks endowed with the thirty-two major characteristics.
Although these marks and signs are accomplished through the Buddha’s merit, they are shadows manifested within the Dharma-body and are not substantial entities;

therefore, it is said that they "should not be" [grasped]. That which is called "not the form-body" and "not the various marks" means that the elemental nature of form and appearance is originally empty;
this is what is called the "form-body. That which is called "the various marks" means that form and appearance are not non-existent.
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall preach some dharma. Do not have such a thought. Why is that?
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has preached some dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha, for they would not understand what I have preached.
Subhūti, as for one who preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; it is called "preaching the Dharma" only by way of designation.
The preceding passage stated that neither the physical body nor its marks and signs can be perceived.
Furthermore, fearing that people might doubt how the Buddha could preach the Dharma if his physical characteristics were non-existent, he said to Subhūti:
"Do not say that the Tathāgata has preached any Dharma. To say that he has preached anything would be to slander the Buddha. Why? Because the Tathāgata has realized all dharmas."
Emptiness is ultimately without grasping. There is no Buddha who can speak, nor is there any Dharma that can be spoken.
If one says there is speaking, would this not be slander? Yet, for what reason is it called "the Buddha speaks"? It is because there is no dharma that can be spoken;
this is what is called "preaching the Dharma."

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Subhūti, those called 'sentient beings'—the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; it is merely a designation."
"Sentient beings.
These sixty-two words originally appear in the Wei edition and are absent from the Qin edition. Now, having examined both commentaries, they both contain an explanation of these words;
therefore, I have also added them here. This doubt concerns the teaching of the Tathāgata, which is "that which is taught without being taught"—the state of non-teaching.
“Dharma! How could sentient beings possibly believe it? The Buddha said, “You think that sentient beings are truly sentient beings;
therefore, they cannot believe. You do not know that these so-called sentient beings are not truly sentient beings, yet they are also not non-sentient beings.
Why are they neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings? It is because of the reason for being a sentient being...”
Those who are called "sentient beings" are all formed through delusive conditions; they are not truly sentient beings, but are merely designated as such.
Since sentient beings are entirely unreal, how can it be said that they are forever incapable of faith and thus opposed to Prajñā?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, is it that there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti.
In my attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained; this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding the three types of *bodhi*:
previously it was stated that there is no dharma by which one attains *bodhi*. Now, a doubt arises as to whether the World-Honored One attained *bodhi* upon becoming a Buddha;

if so, why is it also said that there is "no attainment"? Therefore, this is raised as a question to the Buddha. The Buddha says: "There is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained. This is...
That which is called "bodhi" (enlightenment) refers to the point where deluded attachments are exhausted; this is precisely the fulfillment of awakening.
This differs from the previous statement that "there is truly no dharma by which the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The former was spoken in reference to the causal stage, while this is spoken in reference to the resultant stage. Furthermore, the former merely stated that there is no dharma; this, however, states that there is no dharma [to be attained].
This is called bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because it is without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
Then one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, that which is called "wholesome dharmas" has been taught by the Tathāgata as being non-dharmas;
it is merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
This follows from the preceding statement that not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Because this dharma is equal—neither diminishing in ordinary beings nor increasing in sages, and being devoid of high or low—there is neither attainment nor non-attainment.
To simply realize this dharma of equality is what is called unsurpassed bodhi. Although it is said to be equal, it is not...
It is attained without cultivation. One should cultivate all wholesome dharmas with a mind of non-self and so forth;
thus, conditions will function in unison and the primary and auxiliary practices will be mutually integrated. In this way, one may perhaps hope for Bodhi.

Furthermore, fearing that people might cling to wholesome dharmas as being real and become stuck in the conditioned, the Buddha said: "They are not wholesome dharmas; they are called 'wholesome dharmas'. Within this...

In the preceding passage it was said that nothing is attained; yet later it was said that there is attainment. How are these two statements to be reconciled? Generally speaking, when it is said that there is attainment, it means that one realizes this very state of non-attainment.
Subhūti, suppose all the Sumeru Kings of Mounts within a trichiliocosm were [as numerous as the sands of the Ganges]...
Suppose there were a heap of the seven precious jewels, and someone were to take it and give it as a gift.

If another person were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the former merit would not equal a hundredth part of the latter, nor a thousandth, nor ten-thousandth, nor a hundred-millionth; it would not even be reached by calculation, comparison, or analogy.
The preceding statement said that by practicing various wholesome dharmas through the realization of non-self and non-personhood, one shall attain bodhi.
Among these wholesome dharmas, the upholding of this sutra is the most supreme. Therefore, it further compares the gift of jewels with the merit of upholding the sutra;
for by upholding the sutra, one not only obtains the blessings of wholesome dharmas, but also simultaneously attains the wisdom of non-self.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? Because, in reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," that is not a self; yet ordinary people imagine there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called "ordinary beings" by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary beings; they are merely designated as "ordinary beings.
The preceding statement that "this Dharma is equal, without high or low" may give rise to doubt:

"If all are equal, how is it that the Tathāgata constantly delivers sentient beings? Therefore, the Buddha provides this [teaching] to sever such doubts. You should not say that this is a refutation of a mistaken understanding. Why?
For this reason, the following passage demonstrates right view. From the words "The Tathāgata says there is a self," it proceeds to clarify the absence of self (*anātman*).
Because the Buddha is without self, he does not perceive any sentient beings who can be saved. Although the Buddha occasionally speaks of a self, in reality there is no self;
those who cling to a self are merely ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Although they are called "ordinary worldlings," even these ordinary worldlings do not exist. Ordinary worldlings...
Since even that [self] cannot be apprehended, how could a Tathāgata have a self? A Tathāgata is without self; furthermore, how could there be any sentient beings to be saved?
If this is so, then even if one spends all day saving sentient beings, it does not hinder the equality of the One Way.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is.

The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king would also be a Tathāgata. Subhūti said:
The Buddha said, “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “If one sees me by form, Or seeks me by sound, Such a person follows a deviant path And cannot see the Tathāgata.”
It was previously stated that the physical body (rūpakāya) is not the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people might suspect that because the physical body manifests from the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), the physical body itself must therefore not be the Tathāgata, yet one could nevertheless perceive the Tathāgata through it.
Therefore, he raised the question to Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti), and Subhūti indeed agreed with it. Consequently, the Buddha challenged him by means of the analogy of a Cakravartin King.
This is because it is possible to infer the fundamental from the derivative, but impossible to infer the fundamental from the derivative.
Once Subhūti had realized his error, the Buddha further spoke a verse to clarify it: that the Dharmakāya of True Suchness is not something seen or heard.
That which is reached is the realm of true wisdom; it can only be realized through personal realization.
Therefore, phenomenal forms cannot be observed, and even observation itself cannot be employed. "Observation" (guān) means to examine closely.
Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of marks that are fully complete,
Subhūti, do not think thus. The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of marks that are fully complete.

Since the Buddha has already stated that the Tathāgata cannot be perceived through sound or form, he fears that people, failing to grasp this intent, might seek the Buddha by exclusively negating all characteristics;
therefore, he here prohibits such an approach. For although physical marks are not the Buddha, the Buddha likewise does not exist apart from physical marks.
Subhūti, if you should have this thought: "One who has set out on the path toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speaks of the annihilation and cessation of all dharmas," do not hold such a thought.
Why is that? One who has set out on the path toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation or cessation regarding dharmas.
This statement seeks the Buddha by means of abandoning all characteristics; it is a teaching on the annihilation of all dharmas.
Now, one who seeks Bodhi does not abandon a single dharma among the myriad gates of practice—how could they speak of the dharma of annihilation?

If one speaks of the dharma of annihilation, then within the cause, one will lack the six perfections and the myriad practices; at the stage of the fruit, one will diminish the adornment of merit and virtue. Regarding Bodhi...
They are worlds apart, Subhūti.
If a bodhisattva were to give away as alms the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and if another person were to know that all phenomena are without self and thereby attain the patient endurance [of non-arising], this latter bodhisattva would surpass the former.
Regarding the merit obtained by the Bodhisattva, why is this? Subhūti, it is because Bodhisattvas do not grasp at merit.
Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people, upon hearing this, might misunderstand it as nihilism and thus become attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) or crave that merit;
therefore, he said that although the merit of precious giving is great, it is not called supreme. It is only on the basis of all dharmas that one knows this.
One who has attained patience regarding selflessness is uniquely supreme. Why is he supreme?

Because one who accepts merit possesses inferior merit, whereas one who does not accept merit possesses superior merit. Through patience, one immediately attains the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
The Buddha replied, "Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be grasped with craving; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit."
This explains the meaning of "not receiving. It means that one simply does not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment toward merit;

for this reason, it is said that there is no receiving. If one performs meritorious deeds while giving rise to greedy attachment, then the cause becomes tainted (*sāsrava*), and the fruit will necessarily be tainted.
If one performs meritorious deeds without giving rise to greedy attachment, then the cause becomes untainted (*anāsrava*), and the fruit is likewise untainted. Therefore...
A bodhisattva should not be greedily attached. One who is not greedily attached does so because of the absence of self.
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
He is named Tathāgata.
Previously, it was stated that because a bodhisattva is without self, the merit they obtain surpasses that of bestowing jewels.

Consequently, people came to believe that when a bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, there is actually a real manifestation and the receiving of such merit. Therefore, the Buddha first pointed out this erroneous interpretation, saying:
The Tathāgata has coming and going, sitting and reclining; later, he demonstrates right view by stating that the Tathāgata has no coming and going, nor sitting or reclining.
This is because the Dharma-body is immovable, like empty space, while the Transformation-body appears in response to conditions like a shadow.
If there is appearance, in reality there is no appearance; if there is the receiving of merit, in reality there is no receiving of merit.
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind this trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of dust be great? "It would be very great, World-Honored One. "And why is that?"
If this multitude of atoms were substantially real, the Buddha would not have called it a "multitude of atoms.
Why is that? The Buddha said: "What is called a multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a 'multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata calls a trichiliocosm is not a world; it is merely designated as a "world. For what reason? If the world...
If the realms were truly existent, they would be a "unified mark. The Tathāgata has said that what is called a unified mark is not a unified mark;
it is merely named a unified mark. Subhūti, that which is a unified mark is ultimately ineffable;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.

Regarding the previous statement that one should not be greedily attached: this does not mean that there are characteristics which one simply does not attach to; rather, it means that characteristics are fundamentally empty from the outset.

Therefore, by analyzing and deconstructing the characteristics of the sensory realms, the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of phenomena is revealed. If even subtle atoms were substantially real, [then phenomena would possess intrinsic nature].
The Buddha does not speak of these as "atoms. Why does he not speak of them as atoms? Because the name "atom" is merely a provisional designation.
Atoms have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they are produced by the fragmentation of the elements (*dhātu*). Thus, in reality, they are not atoms;
they are called "atoms" only in name. This is not only true of atoms; it is likewise true of worlds. The world...
The realms have no intrinsic nature; they are not substantially existent, but are merely designated as "worlds.
Why is it that what is not a world is called a "world"? If one were to claim that the world is substantially existent, it would be nothing more than the appearance of a collection of many atoms.
Since it is a conglomeration of many atoms, there is no separate, singular appearance of a "collection" apart from them; it is merely...
It exists as a mere name; emptiness arises herein, and its characteristics have already been dismantled. The Buddha further points this out to the very core, saying:
that which is called a "unified characteristic" (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) is inexpressible.
Since a characteristic is not actually a characteristic, it is the true characteristic (bhūtalakṣaṇa), which cannot be forcibly expressed through language or names. For ordinary beings...
Indeed, those who do not understand take these signs to be real and thus falsely give rise to greed and attachment.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? "No, World-Honored One. This person does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata.
Why is that? Because the World-Honored One has taught: 'the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being...'"

The view of a life-span is not the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span. These are what are called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.

The previous statement that ordinary people who are greedily attached to phenomena do so because they give rise to false attachments regarding the self (*ātman*) and dharmas, now removes this attachment to the self.
This means that if someone says the Tathāgata taught views such as "self" or "person," that person does not understand the meaning of what the Buddha taught.
Why? Because views such as "self" or "person" are fundamentally empty and quiescent; their very substance is [such].

Because it is suchness (*tathatā*), it is said that there is no view of a self, a person, and so forth; yet, following worldly convention, these are provisionally designated as the views of a self, a person, and so forth.
Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, with respect to all phenomena...
Knowing thus, seeing thus, and resolving with faith thus, one does not give rise to the mark of dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called the "mark of dharmas" is, according to the Tathāgata’s teaching, not a mark of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "mark of dharmas."

This is the elimination of attachment to dharmas. That is to say, regarding all dharmas, one knows their mark of non-arising, sees their mark of non-arising, and resolves with faith in their mark of non-arising.
Why is it that they are thus known, seen, and resolved with faith? Because the mark of dharmas is not a mark;
its essence is fundamentally quiescent, and no mark can be apprehended—it is merely designated by the name "mark of dharmas."

Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and takes up this sutra—even just a four-line verse or the like—upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others, their merit would surpass that of the former. How so? For the sake of others...
He preached the Dharma without grasping at signs, remaining as he was, unmoving. Why is this? All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow;
they are like dew and also like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way.
Once the two attachments are exhausted, one naturally enters into silent resonance with True Suchness (*tathatā*) and is thus able to expound this sutra.

Therefore, the Buddha told Subhūti: "The merit of bestowing the seven treasures upon immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds does not equal the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and expounding this sutra for others. How is it that expounding it for others can be so superior?
This is because one does not grasp at marks; it is simply that, being suchness (*tathatā*), one is immovable.
Not grasping at marks means not grasping at the mark of self, not grasping at the mark of dharmas, and also not grasping at the mark of non-dharmas.

When these three marks cannot be apprehended, one can then accord with that true suchness and remain forever without fluctuation. Why is it possible not to grasp at marks? It is simply because one should contemplate the One.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are merely like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning.

These six have no substantial reality at all, yet they falsely appear as if they exist. Because they lack any substantial reality, they can destroy the two marks of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Because they falsely appear as if they exist, they can destroy the mark of non-phenomena (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*). To be able to perform this contemplation is the full meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all those in the world—
gods, humans, asuras, and others— hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
They believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
This is the sutra of the *Kṣānti* (Endurance) chapter. It is the profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sutra, the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

By hearing even a single four-line verse of this sutra, one has already transcended the causes for rebirth in the evil realms; by maintaining it with purity for a single thought-moment, one will certainly receive the prediction of attaining *bodhi*.

Therefore, humans, devas, and all other species were filled with joy. They believed, accepted, and practiced it. As for "believing and accepting": it means not believing in any other phenomena, but believing solely in the *prajñā*.
The practitioner follows the teachings of the sutras to give rise to practice, yet does not grasp at signs; thus they practice while there is no practice.
*A Brief Commentary on the Diamond Sutra* (End).
